title: Orchestrating batch work: DAGs, retries and backfills
goal: By the end, you can say who decides when, how and where a nightly batch job runs, make a job safe to run twice by tying it to one day's data and replacing that day's output, explain why a second copy of a slow task rescues a slow machine but not a big pile of data, and plan a rerun of past days that is safe and leaves room for tonight's jobs.
opening:
Picture the payments company's night shift, run by programs instead of people. After the shops close, three jobs run in turn. One copies in the day's card payments, one works out what each shop is owed, and one writes the report the accountants read at 08:00. One morning, the total for 6 November is twice what the shops took. Every job says it finished fine.

One job had crashed right after saving its total, and the program in charge ran it again. It's easy to trust a retry, because running a failed job again seems careful. That holds only if a job that runs twice leaves what one run leaves.

Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs made each change to a table one commit, whole or not at all. But who starts each job, and what if one starts twice? In this lesson, we'll make jobs wait for each other instead of the clock, make a crashed job safe to rerun, and rerun a year of history. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Every night, a job adds one row to a table called `daily_totals`: the date and the total of that day's payments. One night, the machine running it dies right after the row is saved, before the job can report that it's done. The program in charge sees no "done", so it runs the job again, and this time it finishes. What does `daily_totals` hold for that day?
options: One row: the program in charge undoes a failed attempt before it tries again
Two rows: the day is counted twice
No rows: the attempt that failed is cancelled, row and all
One row: the table refuses a second row for the same day
warmup.why: The first attempt had saved its row before the machine died, so the row stays. The program in charge only knows that the attempt never said "done". It can't undo work a job did in another system, so it runs the job again, and the table accepts a second row. A rule in the table that allows one row per day would make the retry fail instead, which still isn't a working pipeline. The fix is a job that replaces the day's row instead of adding one, so running twice leaves what running once does. The first and third options are the trap: they picture the retry undoing the failed attempt, and nothing does that.

sections.h: Jobs that wait for each other, and three layers that schedule them
sections.body:
Let's start with the night shift. The payments app in this course records every card payment people make at the shops it serves: which card paid, which shop, how much and when. Each night, the company works out what it owes each shop, in three jobs. A job is a program that starts, works through a pile of data and stops.

Job 1 imports a file that the shops' bank sends overnight, listing every payment it really moved money for that day. Banks call this step settlement, so the file is a settlement file. (The code's comments call the shops' bank the acquirer.) Job 2 turns it into settlement lines, one row per payment with the shop, the amount and the company's fee. It runs on Spark, a program that spreads one big job over many machines, because a busy day has millions of rows. Job 3 adds up the lines and writes the report the accountants read at 08:00.

Version 1 uses cron, a scheduler built into Linux and macOS that starts a command at set times. Job 1 starts at 00:30, job 2 at 02:00 and job 3 at 04:00. The gaps are guesses from how long each job usually takes, and that works most nights. But when the bank's file lands two hours late, job 2 starts at 02:00 anyway, on a day that's still half imported. In the Try it, that happens on 2 nights out of 30, and nothing fails, so nobody notices. Cron also doesn't rerun a job that died, doesn't stop a slow run from overlapping the next one, and keeps no record of which day each run was for.

Version 2 writes down what each job needs, and lets a program start each job once the jobs it needs have finished. A restaurant kitchen works this way: the sauce before the plate, and the plate before it goes out. Draw each job as a box and each "must finish before" as an arrow, and you get a **DAG**, a directed acyclic graph. Directed means each arrow points one way. Acyclic means no chain of arrows leads back to where it started, so no job ends up waiting for itself. That's why there's always an order that runs every job after everything it needs, called a topological order.

A program that runs DAGs is a **workflow orchestrator**. The common ones are Apache Airflow (3.4 is current), Dagster and Prefect, all free programs written in Python. Each run of a DAG is for one **logical date**: the day of data it processes, which is different from the moment it runs. The run for 6 November starts in the early hours of 7 November. After a crash it might run at noon, and in a backfill, the last section's topic, months later.

The orchestrator is the top of three layers that each schedule something, as the figure shows. A kitchen has all three. The expediter, who calls each dish when what it needs is ready, is the orchestrator. The cooks, who decide how to cook each dish, are the engine. The manager, who decides which cook works at which station, is the resource manager.

The engine here is Spark, from The Spark execution model. Its main program, the driver, cuts a job into stages, steps that end where data has to move between machines. It cuts each stage into tasks, small pieces of work that each handle one slice of the data. Worker programs called executors run the tasks. When a task fails, the driver reruns it from its lineage, the record of how its input was made, up to 4 attempts in all (`spark.task.maxFailures`). Airflow never sees those tasks.

The resource manager decides which machine runs each program, and how much processor time (CPU) and memory it gets. It manages a cluster, a group of machines that work as one. Clusters built with Hadoop, the first free big data system (HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived), use its resource manager, YARN. Most others use Kubernetes, a program that runs other programs across many machines, each in a sealed box called a container. A Spark driver on Kubernetes asks it for executors, and Kubernetes finds machines with room.

Resource managers have to share. Say a cluster has 160 cores (the parts of a processor that each run one thing at a time), and two jobs each ask for 100. The manager can give each job 80, run one and make the other wait, or take cores from a low-priority job that's already running. Taking them is called preemption, and it kills that job's tasks. Batch work is the usual victim, because it can be redone, and it often runs on cheap rented machines that the cloud company may take back at short notice. On Borg, Google's own cluster manager, preemption killed tasks more often than broken hardware did.

So every layer retries. Next, we'll see what a retry does to a job that had already saved its result.

try.title: Cron's guess against a DAG that waits
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `CronVsDagDemo`. It plays out 30 nights. The bank's file usually lands around 00:30 and sometimes hours late, the import takes 40 to 80 minutes, and the report starts either at 02:00 (cron) or as soon as the import finishes (a DAG). The nights are simulated, so the run takes seconds.
Before you read the output: on how many nights will the cron report be wrong, and will any cron run fail?
Is the DAG's report always later than cron's? Look at the median, the middle time when all 30 are sorted.

code.title: CronVsDagDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l13.demo

import kotlin.random.Random

/**
 * Thirty nights of a two-job pipeline. Job 1 imports the acquirer's settlement file, which usually
 * lands at about 00:30 but some nights is hours late. Job 2 builds the settlement report from it.
 * With cron, job 2 starts at 02:00 every night, a guess that "job 1 is surely done by then". With
 * a DAG, job 2 starts when job 1 finishes.
 */
fun main() {
    val rnd = Random(2026)
    fun clock(m: Int) = "%02d:%02d".format(m / 60, m % 60)
    var wrong = 0
    val cronReady = mutableListOf<Int>()
    val dagReady = mutableListOf<Int>()
    println("night  file lands  import done  cron report (02:00)        DAG report")
    for (night in 1..30) {
        val late = rnd.nextDouble() < 0.1
        val lands = 30 + if (late) 60 + rnd.nextInt(120) else rnd.nextInt(15)
        val imported = lands + 40 + rnd.nextInt(40)                  // the import takes 40 to 80 minutes
        val cronOk = imported <= 120
        if (!cronOk) wrong++
        cronReady += 120 + 10
        dagReady += imported + 10                                     // the report itself takes 10 minutes
        if (!cronOk || night <= 3) {
            println("%5d  %10s  %11s  %-25s  %s".format(night, clock(lands), clock(imported),
                if (cronOk) "${clock(130)}, right" else "${clock(130)}, read a partial day", "${clock(imported + 10)}, right"))
        }
    }
    println("(nights 4 to 30 not shown unless cron got them wrong)")
    println("cron: $wrong of 30 reports built from a partial import; every report ready at ${clock(130)}")
    println("DAG:  0 of 30 wrong; reports ready at a median ${clock(dagReady.sorted()[15])}, the latest at ${clock(dagReady.max())}")
}

try.expect:
```text
night  file lands  import done  cron report (02:00)        DAG report
    1       00:33        01:34  02:10, right               01:44, right
    2       00:41        01:54  02:10, right               02:04, right
    3       00:40        01:35  02:10, right               01:45, right
    4       02:09        03:01  02:10, read a partial day  03:11, right
   25       02:41        03:23  02:10, read a partial day  03:33, right
(nights 4 to 30 not shown unless cron got them wrong)
cron: 2 of 30 reports built from a partial import; every report ready at 02:10
DAG:  0 of 30 wrong; reports ready at a median 01:52, the latest at 03:33
```

On 28 nights the guess of 02:00 was safe. On two nights the file landed after 02:00, so the cron report read a day that was still being imported. Neither run failed, and that's the dangerous part. The DAG started the report when the import finished, so it was never wrong. It was usually earlier than cron, at a median of 01:52. On the two late nights it was later, because there was nothing correct to report before then. The demo uses fixed random numbers, so you get the same nights.

sections.h: A retry is safe only if running twice leaves what running once does
sections.body:
Every layer retries, so every task runs more than once sooner or later. HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived showed when that does no harm. MapReduce, Google's design for one job spread over thousands of machines, reran a lost task on the same input, which never changes. And a task's output became visible only when a rename moved it into place, in one step, so a second attempt could never leave two copies. Inside one engine, those rules hold by design.

The orchestrator's tasks break them, because they write to other systems: a warehouse table, an ordinary database, another company's service. (A warehouse is a database built for questions over years of data.) And the orchestrator can't see inside a task. It knows that an attempt started, and whether it reported success. The case that does the damage is a task that did its writes and then died before it could report. Its machine was taken back, it ran out of memory while tidying up, or the network lost its "done" message. The orchestrator sees a failed attempt and runs the task again.

In the kitchen, it's a cook who plates a steak and is called away before saying "done". The expediter calls the steak again. If the second cook adds another steak to the same plate, the table gets two. If the second cook replaces the plate, it gets one.

The stepper follows one such night, in a pipeline of three tasks. `extract` copies the day's payments into a work table called `staging`. `load` adds them up and writes the total into `daily_totals`. `report` reads it. The night runs twice side by side, into two copies of `daily_totals`. One copy appends a row on every run, with `INSERT INTO`, the command in SQL (the language databases speak) that adds rows. The other replaces the day's partition. A **partition** is one slice of a big table, here one per day, stored apart so a job can read or replace one day without touching the rest. Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore built them.

A task that's safe to retry is **idempotent**: running it twice leaves the same result as running it once. Three rules get you there.

1. Read a fixed input: the partition for the run's logical date. Never "the latest data" or `now()`, the current time, because a retry tomorrow or a backfill next month would read something else.
2. Write by replacing, never by adding. Overwrite the day's partition (`INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION`). Or delete the day and insert it again inside one transaction, a group of changes the database applies all together or not at all. Or use `MERGE`, which updates the rows whose key (here, the day) matches and inserts the rest. Or, in an Iceberg table, kept as files and changed one whole commit at a time, make one commit that replaces the day (Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg). `INSERT INTO` adds another copy on every retry.
3. Make the output appear in one step, so a crash leaves the old result or the new one, never half of each.

**A task that runs twice must leave what one run leaves. Replace the day; never add to it.**

Airflow's best-practices guide says the same in its own words. Use upserts (update the row if it's there, insert it if not) in place of inserts. Read the partition for `data_interval_start`, the start of the run's day, never the latest data. Prefect 3 builds "do this at most once" into its programming interface. You give a piece of work a key, such as its day. When the work commits, Prefect writes a record under that key, and a rerun with the same key finds the record and skips the work.

In the Try it, one night's load crashes right after writing its total. With `INSERT INTO`, the retry writes a second row, and the report shows 11,949,314 cents for a day whose payments add up to 5,974,657. With a partition overwrite, the retry replaces the row and the report is right. Over 90 nights, with a one-in-five chance of such a crash each night, the appending pipeline ends 28% too high. The retry setting alone made the numbers worse.

Retries rerun a task that failed. Some tasks don't fail; they're slow, and everything waits for them. Next, we'll run a second copy on purpose.

try.title: Crash a load after its write, then retry
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `RetryDemo`. It plays one night where the load crashes after writing and is retried, once with a load that appends and once with a load that overwrites the day's partition. Then it plays 90 nights where crashes like that happen at random.
Predict the report for each load before you read the output.
Some nights crashed twice. What does the appending table hold for a night like that?

code.title: RetryDemo.kt (the pipeline is in Model.kt)

try.expect:
```text
load = append (INSERT INTO)
  minute   5  extract   attempt 1: staging has 235 payments, ok
  minute  15  load      attempt 1: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), then the worker died
  minute  20  scheduler retries load after 5 minutes
  minute  30  load      attempt 2: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 2 row(s), ok
  minute  35  report    attempt 1: reports the day as 11,949,314 cents
  the source says 5,974,657 cents
load = overwrite the partition
  minute   5  extract   attempt 1: staging has 235 payments, ok
  minute  15  load      attempt 1: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), then the worker died
  minute  20  scheduler retries load after 5 minutes
  minute  30  load      attempt 2: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), ok
  minute  35  report    attempt 1: reports the day as 5,974,657 cents
  the source says 5,974,657 cents
90 nights, each load crashing after its write with chance 20% (sometimes twice): 21 nights hit
  append    total     720,540,797 cents, +28.0% against the source, 21 wrong days
  overwrite total     563,126,222 cents, +0.0% against the source, 0 wrong days
```

The two pipelines did exactly the same things in the same order. Only the load's write differed. The appending load left one row per attempt, so the report doubled the day. The overwriting load replaced the day's partition on each attempt, so the retry did no harm. Over 90 nights, 21 had a crash of this kind, and the appending pipeline's total ended 28% above the source, the payments themselves. Some nights crashed twice and were counted three times. Every run reported success in the end.

refs.title: Airflow best practices: tasks should be idempotent

aside.title: Why not turn retries off?
aside.body: Then a short network hiccup at 03:00 leaves a day missing until someone notices and reruns the job by hand. Machines are taken back more often than they break, so without retries, missing days would be common. And a rerun by hand is the same second run, with the same doubled row. Making the task safe to run twice fixes the automatic retry and the rerun by hand at once. After that, turn retries on.

sections.h: A second copy of a slow task rescues a slow machine, not a big slice of data
sections.body:
A stage of a batch job finishes when its slowest task finishes, because the next stage needs all of its output. One slow task, called a **straggler**, holds back everything after it. The paper that introduced MapReduce, by two Google engineers in 2004, lists real causes. One machine had a failing disk that read at 1 MB/s instead of 30. Others were busy with other work. And a bug in the start-up code switched off the processor's caches, its small, fast memories, which made some machines more than 100 times slower.

Version 1 is to wait. Without backup tasks, the paper's sort of 1 TB of data took 1,283 seconds instead of 891, which is 44% longer. Its last five tasks alone added about 300 seconds.

Version 2 is the backup task. Near the end of a job, start a second copy of every task that's still running, on another machine, and take whichever copy finishes first. It cost a few percent more computing and removed the slow tail. The same paper also killed 200 of the 1,746 worker programs in the middle of a sort. The job finished in 933 seconds, 5% slower than normal, because their tasks were rerun elsewhere.

Spark calls this **speculative execution**, and it's off by default (`spark.speculation=false`). Switch it on, and Spark checks every 100 ms. It waits until 90% of a stage's tasks have finished (`spark.speculation.quantile`). Then any task running more than 3 times as long as the median task (`spark.speculation.multiplier`) gets a copy on a free slot. The median is the middle time when you sort them, and a slot is a place on an executor that runs one task at a time. Since Spark 3.4, it first checks that the task really is slow for the amount of data it has (`spark.speculation.efficiency.enabled`).

Why off by default? For the last section's reason: two copies of the same task run at the same time. Their output must appear in one step and touch nothing outside. Otherwise a task that writes to a database or calls another company's service does it twice.

And speculation fixes only one kind of straggler. Back in the kitchen, if one cook is slow because the stove is weak, a second cook on a good stove makes the same dish and wins. If the dish is slow because it's a roast for forty people, the second cook needs just as long. In Spark's terms, when the machine is slow, the copy runs on a healthy machine and wins. When the task is slow because its slice of data is big, the copy reads the same big slice and is just as slow.

That second case is skew, from The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching. Spark sends rows to tasks by a key, such as the shop's id. When one key is very common, say one huge shop with 30% of the rows, one task gets 30% of the work. The fix is to split that key. AQE, the part of Spark that rethinks a query's steps while it runs, can split it for a join (matching rows from two tables). Or you can salt the key: add a random number to it, so its rows spread over several tasks. Running the same task twice splits nothing.

In the Try it, one slow machine stretched a 40-second stage to 120 seconds, and speculation brought it back to 48. One skewed task stretched it to 144 seconds, and speculation started a copy that changed nothing.

Retries and backup copies rerun a few tasks at a time. Next, we'll rerun months of runs, on purpose.

try.title: Speculate on a slow machine and on a skewed task
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `SpeculationDemo`. It plays one stage of 200 tasks on 20 slots, in simulated seconds. In one case a machine (2 slots) is 30 times slower; in the other, one task holds 30 times the data. Each case runs without and with Spark's speculation rule.
Predict which case speculation rescues before you read the table.
Read the `stage` function. When does the rule start copying tasks, and which copy wins?

code.title: SpeculationDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
stage of 200 tasks, 20 slots           no speculation        speculation
one slow machine (2 slots, 30x)              120.0 s            48.0 s   (2 speculative copies)
one skewed task (30x the data)               144.0 s           144.0 s   (1 speculative copy)
a healthy stage takes 40.0 s
```

From outside, the two cases look the same: a stage that should take 40 seconds takes two or three times as long because of one or two tasks. Speculation tells them apart. On the slow machine, the two tasks that landed there got copies on healthy slots, which finished long before the originals: 48 seconds. The skewed task's copy had the same 30 times more data to work through, so it was no faster, and the stage still took 144 seconds. The times are simulated, so they're the same on every computer.

sections.h: Rerunning past days with a backfill, and what makes it safe
sections.body:
Say a bug in the fee calculation was live for 90 days. Fixing the code fixes tonight's numbers, but the past 90 days are still wrong, and each has to be worked out again. Running a DAG for past logical dates like that is a **backfill**, and every day of history becomes one run. You need one too when a new report needs a year of data, or old rows need a new column filled in.

Airflow 3 runs backfills itself, started from its web page, its programming interface or the command line:

```bash
airflow backfill create --dag-id settlement \
    --from-date 2026-08-09 --to-date 2026-11-06 \
    --reprocess-behavior completed --max-active-runs 8
```

`--reprocess-behavior` says which days to run. `none` runs only days that have no run yet, `failed` adds days whose run failed, and `completed` reruns every day. `--max-active-runs` caps how many of the backfill's runs go at once, and it matters more than it looks. Airflow's documentation says the scheduler doesn't put backfill tasks behind other work. So a backfill with no cap competes on equal terms with tonight's runs. `--run-backwards` does the newest days first.

The arithmetic works in waves, rounds of runs that go side by side. A year of daily runs of 20 minutes each, 16 at a time, takes 23 waves (365 divided by 16, rounded up): about 7.7 hours. Run backwards, the newest week is ready after 20 minutes, which is usually what people are waiting for.

Whether a backfill is safe is decided by the tasks, not by the orchestrator. It's safe when every run reads only its own logical date's input and replaces its own output. Then running a day twice changes nothing, and `--reprocess-behavior completed` does no harm. It's unsafe in three common ways. A task that appends doubles every day it reruns, as the Try it shows. A task that reads "the latest partition" or `now()` gets today's data in every past run; the lab has one, and it copies today's total into all 90 backfilled days. And a task with an outside effect, such as an email to each shop or a call to a partner company's service, repeats it for every day.

Here our kitchen picture breaks. A kitchen can't cook last month's dinners again. A pipeline can work out any past day again. It needs that day's input still stored, and each run must read only that day and replace only that day's output.

The newer orchestrators move the unit of work from tasks to data. In Airflow 3, a task can declare the **assets** it updates, meaning the tables or files it writes, and another DAG can run whenever one of them changes. Dagster is built around software-defined assets. You declare each table, and the function that computes it from the tables it reads. Running that function and storing the result is called materializing the asset. Give an asset one partition per day, and a backfill becomes "materialize these 90 partitions". That works only if each partition is computed from its own inputs and replaced whole. Prefect 3 (3.9 is current) stays closer to plain Python: flows and tasks are ordinary functions marked `@flow` and `@task`.

That's also where all of this stops. The orchestrator can rerun any task, but it can't tell whether a rerun is safe. That's decided in each task's code, and an email that went out can't be taken back.

try.title: Size a year's backfill, then run it twice
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `BackfillDemo`. It schedules 365 daily runs of 20 minutes with 1, 4 and 16 runs at a time, oldest first and backwards. Then it runs the whole backfill twice with each kind of load.
Before you read: how long does 16 at a time take? Work it out as waves.
Which number would the accountants care about first, the total time or the time until the newest week is ready?

code.title: BackfillDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
365 daily runs of 20 minutes:
  max active runs  1: done after 121.7 h; the newest week is ready after 121.7 h, or   2.3 h with run backwards
  max active runs  4: done after  30.7 h; the newest week is ready after  30.7 h, or   0.7 h with run backwards
  max active runs 16: done after   7.7 h; the newest week is ready after   7.7 h, or   0.3 h with run backwards
backfill run twice, load = append    total is 2.00 times the source
backfill run twice, load = overwrite total is 1.00 times the source
```

The total time is waves times run time. 365 divided by 16, rounded up, is 23 waves of 20 minutes: 7.7 hours, if the cluster really has room for 16 runs at once. Oldest first, the newest week is ready only at the very end; backwards, it's ready in the first wave. Running the whole backfill a second time, which is what `--reprocess-behavior completed` does after a partial failure, doubled the appending pipeline's numbers. The overwriting pipeline's stayed exactly right.

mistake: The common mistake is turning on retries, or running a backfill, for tasks that append. A setting like `retries=3` feels like safety, so it goes into every DAG, and nothing looks wrong: each run ends as succeeded. But every attempt that died after its write leaves its rows behind, and the next attempt adds them again. The tables creep upward a few nights a month, and a backfill with `--reprocess-behavior completed` doubles a whole quarter at once. It happens because most tasks start life as scripts meant to run once, and `INSERT INTO` is the natural way to write one. The fix is in the task, not the orchestrator. Read the logical date's partition, replace that date's output in one step, and move outside effects such as emails into a separate task that records what it already did. Then turn retries on.

worked.title: Turn a cron script into a DAG that's safe to retry and backfill

steps.say: Start from what runs today: a line for cron and a script that totals "yesterday" and appends the result. `0 2 * * *` means minute 0 of hour 2, every day. `current_date` is today's date, so the script works relative to the clock. A rerun on any other day computes the wrong day, and a rerun on the same day doubles it.
steps.code:
# crontab: 02:00 every night
0 2 * * * /opt/jobs/daily_totals.sh

-- daily_totals.sh runs this SQL
INSERT INTO daily_totals (day, total_cents)
SELECT current_date - 1, sum(amount_cents)
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= current_date - 1 AND created_at < current_date;

steps.say: Make the day a parameter. The orchestrator passes the run's logical date in as `:day` (Airflow fills in `{{ ds }}` with it). Now the run for 6 November computes 6 November, whether it runs that night, after a retry, or in a backfill months later.
steps.code:
-- :day is the run's logical date (Airflow's {{ ds }} or data_interval_start)
SELECT :day, sum(amount_cents)
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= :day AND created_at < :day + INTERVAL '1 day';

steps.say: Replace instead of append, inside one transaction, so the delete and the insert happen together or not at all. A crash leaves the old row or the new one, and a rerun writes the same single row again.

Put it in a DAG, with its dependency on the import and with retries, which are now safe. The `@dag` and `@task` markers come from Airflow 3's task kit, `airflow.sdk`, and `>>` says "import before load". The comment's acquirer is the shops' bank, which sends the file.

Work out again the 90 days a bug was live: a backfill, capped at 8 runs at a time so tonight's runs still get their turn, and newest first so this week's numbers are fixed first. Every run replaces its own day, so running it again after a partial failure does no harm.

lab.title: A DAG runner with retries and backfills, on virtual time
steps: Run the tests. All 13 fail on `TODO`s. Read `Warehouse.kt` and `PaymentTasks.kt` first. The pipeline is extract (5 minutes), load (10) and report (5), and `Faults` makes chosen attempts crash right after their writes.

Exercise 1, `Dag.topologicalOrder`: find an order that runs every task after the tasks it needs, with Kahn's algorithm. Count each task's unfinished dependencies, keep the tasks that are ready (a count of 0) in id order, and throw `IllegalArgumentException` if some tasks never become ready. That means there's a cycle.

Exercise 2, `DagRunner.run`: run the tasks in that order on a clock that starts at `startMinute`. A task whose dependencies didn't all succeed is `UPSTREAM_FAILED` and never runs. Each attempt adds the task's minutes. A failed attempt waits `retryDelayMinutes` and tries again, up to `maxRetries` retries.
Exercise 3, `DagRunner.backfill`: `maxActiveRuns` slots, with each day given to the slot that's free earliest. The timing test expects 23 waves of 20 minutes for 90 days at 4 runs at a time.

Exercise 4, `overwriteDailyTotal`: the load that's safe to run twice. Then look at what the append test proves about the given `appendDailyTotal`, and at the test where `latestDailyTotal` copies today into every backfilled day.

Run until all 13 pass. The last one is a property test, written with jqwik, a library that runs one test on many random inputs. It tries 30 random crash patterns, and your overwrite load must match the source every time.
hints: For Kahn's algorithm: `waiting = tasks.associate { it.id to it.deps.size }`, `dependents` grouped by dependency, `ready = sortedSetOf<String>()`. Take `ready.first()`, append it, lower the count of each of its dependents, and add those that reach 0. If the order is shorter than the task list, there's a cycle.

In `run`, wrap the action: `runCatching { task.action(RunContext(logicalDate, attempt, warehouse)) }.isSuccess`. The first attempt plus `maxRetries` retries means `attempt > maxRetries` is the last one. Record the attempts per task, 0 for a task that never ran.
In `backfill`, `val freeAt = LongArray(maxActiveRuns)`; for each day `val slot = freeAt.indices.minBy { freeAt[it] }`, run with `startMinute = freeAt[slot]`, then set `freeAt[slot]` to the run's end.
The idempotent load is one line different from the given append: `ctx.warehouse.overwrite("daily_totals", ctx.logicalDate, listOf(total))`.

drill.title: Make a nightly task safe to retry
drill.prompt: This task runs every night and is retried when it fails. `settlement_lines` holds one row per payment the bank has settled: the shop (`merchant_id`), the fee the company kept (`fee_cents`) and when the money moved (`settled_at`). The task adds up each shop's fees: `INSERT INTO fee_totals SELECT merchant_id, sum(fee_cents) FROM settlement_lines WHERE settled_at >= now() - INTERVAL '1 day' GROUP BY merchant_id`. From memory, name its two problems, and rewrite it so that a retry, or a backfill of any past day, leaves the right numbers. Use `:day` for the run's logical date.

recap: Three layers schedule batch work. The workflow orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect) decides when each job runs, in what order and for which day. The engine (Spark's driver) splits a job into tasks and reruns the ones that fail. The resource manager (Kubernetes, YARN) decides which machine runs each program.
A DAG writes down which job needs which, so a job starts when its input is complete instead of at a guessed time. Every run is for one logical date, the day of data it processes.

Every layer retries, so every task must be idempotent: read only the logical date's partition (never the latest data or `now()`), replace that day's output in one step, and keep outside effects such as emails in their own task, with a record of what was done.

Speculative execution starts a copy of a slow task on another machine. It rescues a slow machine and does nothing for skew, where the copy reads the same big slice. Spark leaves it off by default because both copies run.

A backfill runs the DAG for past days. Cap it with `--max-active-runs` (backfill tasks don't wait behind tonight's), size it in waves, run it backwards to get recent days first, and expect `--reprocess-behavior completed` to rerun days that already succeeded.
The limit: the orchestrator can rerun any task, but it can't tell whether a rerun is safe. That's decided in each task's code, and a sent email can't be taken back.
closing:
We started with a total for 6 November twice as large as the shops' real takings, though every job said it had finished fine. The load died after saving its row, the orchestrator ran it again, and `INSERT INTO` added the same total twice. A load that replaces its day makes that retry harmless, and a year's backfill too.

On a Mac or Linux computer, run `crontab -l` in a terminal. It lists the commands cron starts for you on a timer; most people have none. For any line, ask what happens if it runs twice, or not at all.

Next, we'll follow these nightly results: what are they for, and how does a whole night's output reach a live app at once?

quiz.q: An Airflow task starts a Spark job, which runs on Kubernetes. Halfway through a stage, one executor (a worker program that runs Spark's tasks) is lost. Who reruns the lost tasks?
options: Airflow, which retries the whole task
Kubernetes, which restarts the executor with the same tasks inside
Spark's driver, which reruns those tasks on other executors from their lineage
Nobody: the stage fails and the job must be started again
quiz.why: Tasks belong to the engine's layer. Spark's driver notices the lost executor, asks Kubernetes for room if it needs it, and reruns the missing tasks from their lineage, up to `spark.task.maxFailures` attempts each. Airflow sees nothing unless the whole Spark job fails. Kubernetes only places programs on machines; it doesn't know what a task is. The first option is tempting because Airflow is the program you saw start the job.

quiz.q: From The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching: in a join stage, one task runs for 40 minutes while 199 finish in 30 seconds. Spark's web page shows that this one task read 30% of the data. A teammate sets `spark.speculation=true`. What happens?
options: Spark starts a copy of the long task on another executor; the copy reads the same 30% and is just as slow
The copy finishes in about 30 seconds, like the other tasks
Spark splits the big task into smaller ones
Nothing: speculation only works when Spark may add executors while it runs
quiz.why: The task is slow because of its data, one very common key, not because of its machine. A copy works through the same oversized slice, so it loses the race or ties. Splitting the slice is what AQE's skew join or salting do, as that lesson showed; speculation can't split anything. The second option is the trap: it pictures the copy getting a smaller share of the work.

quiz.q: You need to backfill 180 days. Each run takes 30 minutes, and you set `--max-active-runs 12`. Roughly how long does it take, if the cluster has room for 12 runs at once?
options: 30 minutes
7.5 hours
15 hours
90 hours
quiz.why: 180 divided by 12 is 15 waves, each 30 minutes long: 450 minutes, or 7.5 hours. 90 hours is all the runs one after another, and 15 hours counts each wave as 60 minutes instead of 30. Run backwards, the most recent days are done in the first wave.

quiz.q: Which daily task is safe to run again for any past day?
options: It appends the day's totals to a table with a rule that allows one row per `(day, merchant_id)`
It totals the newest partition of `payments` and overwrites the run's day
It reads the run's own day of `payments` and replaces that day's partition of the output in one step
It emails each shop its totals, then writes them to the table
quiz.why: Only the third reads a fixed input and replaces a fixed output, so running it again changes nothing. The one-row rule (a unique index) turns a retry into an error rather than a right answer. Reading the newest partition puts today's data into every past day of a backfill. And the email goes out again on every run, whatever the table does.

quiz.q: A task calls a partner company's service to report each shop's daily total, then writes the totals to the warehouse. It runs out of time after the calls and is retried. What's the right fix?
options: Raise the retry count so it succeeds in the end
Turn off retries for this task
Write the totals first, and make the calls in a separate task that skips shops and days already recorded as sent
Run it with speculative execution so a second copy finishes first
quiz.why: The call to the partner is the part that can't be undone or overwritten, so it gets its own task. That task keeps a record of what it has sent, by day and shop, and skips those on a rerun. It's the batch version of an idempotency key, a unique id that makes a repeated request do nothing. More retries repeat the calls more often. No retries turns a brief timeout into a missing day. Speculation would make the calls twice on purpose.

flashcards.front: Which three layers schedule batch work, and what does each decide?
flashcards.back: The orchestrator: when each job runs, in what order, for which day. The engine: a job's stages and tasks, and their retries. The resource manager: which machine runs each program, with how much CPU and memory.

flashcards.front: What is a run's logical date?
flashcards.back: The day of data the run processes, which isn't when it runs. The run for 6 November may run that night, after a retry, or in a backfill months later.

flashcards.front: What makes a batch task idempotent?
flashcards.back: It reads a fixed input (its logical date's partition) and replaces a fixed output (that date's partition) in one step, so running it again leaves the same result.

flashcards.front: Why does `INSERT INTO` plus retries count a day twice?
flashcards.back: An attempt that dies after its write, but before it reports success, leaves its rows behind, and the retry adds them again.
When a task is slow because of its machine (a failing disk, a busy machine). Not when its slice of data is big: the copy reads the same data.

flashcards.front: What do `--reprocess-behavior` and `--max-active-runs` control in an Airflow 3 backfill?
flashcards.back: Which days rerun (`none`, `failed` or `completed`), and how many backfill runs go at once. Backfill tasks don't wait behind tonight's runs, so the cap protects them.

flashcards.front: How long do 365 daily runs of 20 minutes take with 16 at a time?
flashcards.back: 365 / 16, rounded up, is 23 waves of 20 minutes: about 7.7 hours.

terms.plain: A directed acyclic graph: jobs or tasks as boxes, "must finish before" as one-way arrows, and no loops, so there's always an order to run them in.
A program that starts whole jobs in the order their dependencies allow, retries them and records each run, such as Airflow, Dagster or Prefect.
The day of data a run is for, whenever the run actually happens.
One slice of a big table, such as one day, stored apart so a job can read or replace it alone.
A task that leaves the same result whether it runs once or many times.
Running a pipeline for past logical dates, to fill in or work out history again.
A task much slower than the rest of its stage, which holds back everything after it.
Starting a copy of a slow task on another machine and keeping whichever copy finishes first.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why the daily totals ended 28% too high after three months of nightly runs that all showed success, and what you changed so that retries and backfills are safe.
explain_back.answer: Every run showed success because every task succeeded in the end, but some of them only on their second or third attempt. The load task added the day's total as a new row with INSERT INTO. On some nights, the machine running it died after the row was saved but before the task could report that it was done. The orchestrator saw a failed attempt and ran the task again, and the retry added the same total a second time. Nights that crashed twice were counted three times. Nothing failed, so nothing warned us; the numbers crept up. The retries only showed that the task wasn't safe to run twice. We changed the task in two ways. It now reads only the partition for its logical date, never the latest data or the current time, so every rerun of 6 November sees the same input. And it replaces that day's output in one step (delete the day and insert it inside one transaction, or overwrite the partition) instead of adding to it, so a second attempt leaves exactly what the first one did. With that, retries are safe. We then backfilled the whole quarter with reprocess set to completed to repair the history, newest days first, with a cap on runs at once so the nightly jobs kept running.

deeper.body:
Resource managers repay a closer look if you ever run your own cluster. YARN splits its work into a central ResourceManager, a NodeManager on every machine, and one ApplicationMaster per job that asks for containers on the job's behalf. Kubernetes has a scheduler, a kubelet (an agent) on every machine, and operators, add-on programs that play the ApplicationMaster's part. On Kubernetes, Spark's driver runs in a pod, Kubernetes's name for one or more containers that run together, and asks the Kubernetes API for executor pods; Spark 4.3's documentation lists Kubernetes 1.34 or newer. The kubelet runs each pod inside cgroups, the Linux feature from the Operating systems track that caps a program's CPU and memory. Both resource managers keep their own state in a coordination service (ZooKeeper for YARN's high availability, etcd for Kubernetes), which the Consistency and consensus track covers.

Some jobs need all their containers at once or none. Spark executors and machine learning jobs are like that, since half of them can sit waiting for the other half. Placing a whole group at once is called gang scheduling. The default Kubernetes scheduler places pods one at a time, which is why Spark's documentation names batch schedulers such as Volcano and Apache YuniKorn.

Preemption changes how you size jobs. Tasks on spot or preemptible machines (cheap capacity a cloud company can take back) get killed often, so you want many small tasks: the MapReduce paper ran 200,000 map tasks on 2,000 machines. You also want output that survives a lost executor. Spark's graceful decommissioning (`spark.decommission.enabled`) moves shuffle and cached blocks off an executor that's about to be removed, and remote shuffle services keep shuffle data outside the executors entirely.

Orchestrators keep moving toward data. Airflow 3 added DAG versioning, so a run finishes on the code it started with, and scheduling driven by events on top of assets. Dagster's partitioned assets make "which days of this table are out of date?" a question the orchestrator can answer. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition) covers job orchestration, preemption and workflows in chapter 11.
